title: The Oresteia
author: Aeschylus
openingText: I pray the gods to quit me of my toils, to close the watch I keep, this livelong year; for as a watch-dog lying, not at rest, propped on one arm, upon the palace-roof of Atreus' race, too long, too well I know the starry conclave of the midnight sky, too well, the splendours of the firmament, the lords of light, whose kingly aspect shows what time they set or climb the sky in turn, the year's divisions, bringing frost or fire. And now, as ever, am I set to mark when shall stream up the glow of signal-flame, the bale-fire bright, and tell its Trojan tale — Troy town is ta'en: such issue holds in hope she in whose woman's breast beats heart of man.
about:
The Oresteia is the only complete Greek trilogy that has survived — three plays by Aeschylus, performed in 458 BCE, telling the story of Agamemnon's family across two generations. In the first play, Clytemnestra murders her husband Agamemnon on his return from Troy. In the second, their son Orestes returns and kills Clytemnestra and her lover. In the third, the Furies pursue Orestes for the killing of his mother — until Athena establishes the first court of human justice in Athens to break the cycle of vengeance.

Aeschylus wrote the trilogy a few years before his death. It is the founding work of Western drama as we know it. The argument it stages — that human civilization required the replacement of blood-vengeance with public justice — is the foundational claim of legal and political order in the West.

angleCards.title: From revenge to justice.
angleCards.text: The trilogy is structured as a transformation: blood revenge (Agamemnon) demands blood revenge (The Libation Bearers), until the cycle becomes impossible to close (The Eumenides). Athena's court does not simply acquit Orestes — it replaces the logic of retaliation with the logic of deliberation. Watch how Aeschylus builds the pressure until no individual act of killing can resolve it.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the trilogy's structural arc — how Aeschylus takes us from the logic of blood revenge to the founding of the first court — and ask what that transformation costs.

angleCards.title: Clytemnestra: Aeschylus's most original creation.
angleCards.text: Clytemnestra dominates the first play in ways no female character in earlier Greek literature does. She is strategist, orator, deceiver, and killer — and Aeschylus gives her arguments that are not easily dismissed. She killed a man who killed her daughter. Pay attention to how the Chorus responds to her: they keep trying to disbelieve her, and she keeps being right.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Agamemnon as Clytemnestra's play — tracking how Aeschylus constructs a female protagonist who is simultaneously monstrous and fully justified, and how the men around her cannot process what she is.

angleCards.title: The Furies and the birth of law.
angleCards.text: The Furies are not villains. They are the oldest moral logic there is: blood demands blood, the debt must be paid, the killer must suffer. Athena does not destroy them — she persuades them to accept a new role. The Eumenides is a courtroom drama that is also a negotiation between two entirely coherent systems of justice. Ask which one you find more compelling.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read The Eumenides as a genuine philosophical debate between two systems of justice — the Furies' logic of retribution and Athena's logic of deliberation — and decide whether Aeschylus fully resolves the tension or leaves it open.

angleCards.title: Cassandra's scene: foresight as suffering.
angleCards.text: The most celebrated scene in Agamemnon belongs to a woman who is already a prisoner and has already accepted she will die. Cassandra sees what is about to happen in the palace and tells the Chorus — who do not believe her, because the gods cursed her to be disbelieved. She names what is coming with complete accuracy and walks through the door anyway. This is the most famous scene of foresight in Greek tragedy.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to focus on Cassandra's scene as the emotional and moral centre of Agamemnon — a woman who sees clearly, speaks truthfully, and is heard by no one — and ask what Aeschylus is saying about the relationship between knowledge and power.

cast.name: Agamemnon
cast.description: Commander of the Greek forces at Troy, now returning after ten years of war. He does not appear until late in the first play, and when he does, he is already walking into a house that has been prepared for him.

cast.name: Clytemnestra
cast.description: Agamemnon's wife, who has governed Argos alone during the decade of war. She is the dominant figure of the first play — a woman of formidable intelligence and patience, who has had ten years to plan.

cast.name: Cassandra
cast.description: Daughter of Priam, now Agamemnon's captive, brought home from Troy as a war prize. Apollo gave her the gift of prophecy and then cursed her so that no one would believe her. She sees what is inside the palace before she enters it.

cast.name: Orestes
cast.description: Son of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra, sent away from Argos as a child. He is the protagonist of the second and third plays, charged by Apollo with an act that is simultaneously a sacred duty and an unforgivable crime.

cast.name: The Furies
cast.description: Ancient goddesses who pursue those who shed kindred blood. They appear in the third play as Orestes' accusers — relentless, correct by their own logic, and older than the Olympian gods who are trying to supersede them.

cast.name: Athena
cast.description: She arrives in the final play to resolve a crisis that no mortal and no other god can settle. Her solution is not a verdict but an institution: a human jury, a formal trial, a new way of deciding what justice requires.

whyItMatters.title: The Founding of Justice
whyItMatters.body: The trilogy ends with the establishment of the Areopagus — the first court of law — to settle Orestes's case. The myth dramatizes the argument that civilization required taking vengeance out of private hands. The argument was new in 458 BCE and is still alive in any debate about state violence.

whyItMatters.title: The Cycle of Blood
whyItMatters.body: The first two plays show how vengeance breeds vengeance — Agamemnon's daughter sacrificed to start a war, Agamemnon murdered for it, his wife murdered in return. The trilogy is a study in why families and societies cannot end this kind of pattern alone. They need outside arbitration to break out.

whyItMatters.title: The Furies Are Not Wrong
whyItMatters.body: The Furies, who hound Orestes, are not portrayed as evil. They are the ancient law of blood. The trilogy is honest that the new justice does not replace the old one cleanly. The Furies are renamed the Eumenides — the kindly ones — and given a place under the new order. Justice does not eliminate them; it incorporates them.
